articleSummary: Tick fever (scrub typhus) is an acute infection caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, transmitted by chigger bites. Examination found an eschar with a dry, dark crust in the axilla; combined with exposure history and disease progression, she was diagnosed and started on antibiotics and antipyretics after one day. Not all patients have eschar; some present with rash, lymphadenopathy, or nonspecific fever. The disease is linked to grassy, bushy, humid environments and higher risk for forest workers, farmers, and gardeners. Complications include acute kidney injury, liver injury, multi-organ involvement, and altered consciousness. Prevention: wear long clothing, cover limbs, and inspect skin after outdoor work; seek care for fever of unknown origin and report exposure. Bach Mai Hospital notes it has saved many scrub typhus cases from severe outcomes.

articleSummary: Influenza A cases are rising, with hospitals reporting surges as infections increase. Influenza is a seasonal respiratory virus; Influenza A, along with B, C, and D, drives most human disease and outbreaks. The circulating strain is Influenza A (H1N1), descended from the 2009 pandemic virus and continues to mutate seasonally. Transmission occurs via droplets, saliva, or contaminated surfaces. After exposure, the incubation is 1–3 days, and symptoms usually appear 3–7 days post-exposure (often around day 3). Common symptoms include high fever, dry cough, sore throat, congestion, fatigue, headache, loss of appetite, nausea, and muscle/joint pains; diarrhea can occur. Severe complications include fever above 38°C for more than a week, pneumonia, shortness of breath, tachycardia, hypotension, respiratory failure, and febrile seizures in children. Most recover in 4–7 days with treatment; if no improvement after a week, further evaluation is needed. Maintain health precautions and immune support amid rising Influenza A activity.

articleSummary: Influenza A remains a concern in Jogja (Yogyakarta), Indonesia, with circulating subtypes A(H1N1)pdm09 and A(H3N2). The influenza virus spreads mainly via coughing, sneezing, and contaminated surfaces, with an incubation of about two days (1–4 days possible). People are most contagious during the first three days after symptoms begin, though transmission can occur from one day before illness onset to five to seven days after. Typical symptoms include fever, dry cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, headache, body aches, fatigue, and sometimes nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea (more common in children). Most recover in about a week, but pneumonia and complications can occur, especially in children under 5 (particularly under 2), older adults, pregnant women, and those with chronic or immunosuppressive conditions. Severe warning signs require medical care; antivirals may help if started early, and vaccination remains a key preventive measure.

articleSummary: Harvest mites (trombiculos), officially named trombiculid mites and also known as red ticks, are proliferating in England as autumn approaches. These tiny parasites, under 0.5 mm, live in soil and dense vegetation and attach to people and animals. Larvae surge in September–October when eggs hatch, with bites typically noticed about 24 hours later. In humans, the resulting wheals and itching usually resolve in one to two weeks; in animals, epithelial-cell feeding and saliva provoke intense pruritus, causing scratching and skin wounds that can become bacterial or fungal infections. Metro reports these mites can transmit diseases to humans; by contrast, East Asia–Pacific relatives may cause scrub typhus, a potentially fatal illness. Bites commonly affect the waist, ankles, and skin folds, while pets are frequently affected on the legs, abdomen, and head.

articleHeadline: Breaking the cycle of hepatitis B in the Philippines
articleSummary: World Hepatitis Day highlights hepatitis B in the Philippines, among the Pacific’s endemic countries. 7.3 million Filipino adults (≈17% of adults) live with chronic HBV, more than double the regional average. HBV can be acute or chronic; many infections are asymptomatic for years but chronic infection can progress to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer. Vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention: a birth dose within 24 hours followed by Program on Immunization offers protection for at least 20 years. Perinatal transmission remains a leading route; antiviral therapy in pregnant women reduces the risk to newborns. Newborns receive birth dose, and exposed infants get immunoglobulin and vaccination. Thailand’s universal newborn vaccination since 1992, with screening and immunoglobulin for exposed infants, reduced carrier rates to below 0.1% and shows progress toward elimination by 2030. Expanded screening in the Philippines is urged for early diagnosis and timely antiviral treatment to prevent liver disease.

articleSummary: Marburg virus disease is a deadly, rare hemorrhagic fever caused by Marburgvirus. Symptoms start with fever, malaise, and body aches and can progress to severe bleeding and organ failure. First identified in 1967 after outbreaks in Germany and Serbia linked to a shipment of infected African green monkeys from Uganda, causing seven deaths. Outbreaks have occurred in Uganda, Angola, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Kenya, Guinea, Equatorial Guinea, Ghana, and Tanzania. Transmission occurs from animals to humans—primarily via African fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus) in caves or mines—and between people through body fluids or contaminated objects; sexual transmission via semen may occur weeks after recovery. Incubation ranges 2 days to 3 weeks; symptoms typically appear about a week after infection. Fatality ranges 23-90%, with deaths about 8–9 days after onset. Diagnosis relies on ELISA or PCR; no approved cure exists; prevention relies on PPE and safe handling.

articleSummary: Handwashing with soap and water is a simple, cost-effective defense against infectious disease. In Vietnam, the Ministry of Health promotes routine hand hygiene in hospitals and communities, prescribing a six-step technique and at least 30 seconds of washing—covering palms, backs, between fingers, and under nails—followed by drying. The Ho Chi Minh City CDC says soap and water remain superior; alcohol-based sanitizers should be used only when soap and water are unavailable. Sanitizers with at least 60% alcohol help in certain situations but do not remove all germs, may be less effective on dirty hands, and can contain harmful additives. Wash before meals and after toilet or after contact with public surfaces; keep sanitizer away from children.

Subtypes are defined by surface proteins hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N): H1–H18 and N1–N11, with over 130 natural combinations observed and more generated by reassortment between different subtypes. articleHeadline: 가슴에 생긴 혹, 암 아닌 '기생충'이었다... 60대 여성이 겪은 일은?
articleSummary: 65-year-old woman in the Democratic Republic of the Congo presented with a chest lump that persisted for seven years. Surgical excision and histopathology confirmed subcutaneous cysticercosis due to Taenia solium larvae, with the scolex observed inside the mass. This non-neural manifestation contrasts with neurocysticercosis, and the lesion resembled a soft tissue tumor. Complete removal obviated the need for antiparasitic therapy, and one-year follow-up showed no symptoms. Authors caution that long-standing, non-changing subcutaneous nodules can be caused by cysticercosis and should be considered in differential diagnoses in endemic regions. Transmission likely occurs via ingestion of eggs from contaminated food or water or poor hygiene, with fecal-oral spread; emphasis on hand hygiene and sanitary handling of food and water. Case published in International Journal of Surgical Case Reports (2026-09-18).

articleSummary: Thrissur district, Kerala, India, reports an ongoing mumps outbreak as of 19 September 2026. The viral illness spreads mainly through airborne droplets and close contact. The hallmark symptom is swelling under the ear due to parotid gland involvement, which may affect one or both sides. Early symptoms include low-grade fever, headache, pain while opening the mouth or chewing, drooling, loss of appetite, and fatigue. The contagious period extends from two days before parotitis to four to six days after onset. Although children aged 5–15 years are most affected, adults can also be ill and may experience more severe disease. Complications can involve the brain, testes, pancreas, and possibly other organs. Precautionary measures: alert teachers and health workers, keep infected children at home, disinfect items used by patients, wear masks, maintain social distancing, and wash hands with soap.

articleHeadlineTranslated: African swine fever threatens to wipe out several species: not only pigs are at risk.
articleHeadline: La peste suina africana minaccia di far estinguere alcune specie: non solo maiali a rischio
articleSummary: ASF emerged in China in late 2018 and has spread across Asia-Pacific, threatening Asia’s rare wild suids. A Nature Reviews Biodiversity analysis warns the virus could push several island-endemic populations toward extinction within a single generation. The authors propose an eight-point plan to safeguard 12 endemic Asian suid species, with urgent actions including rapid outbreak detection, securing reproductive stocks in captivity, and sustained funding. In the wild, ASF has been confirmed in four species—Sulawesi babirusa (Babyrousa celebensis), Sulawesi wild boar (Sus celebensis), Philippine warty pig (Sus philippensis), and bearded pig (Sus barbatus)—with strong suspicion in Visayan warty pig (Sus cebifrons) and Mindoro warty pig (Sus oliveri). On Sulawesi, both babirusa and boar are affected; the babirusa is evolutionarily distinct, with tusks that grow through the snout. In Borneo, bearded pig declines affect local communities; wild suids contribute to soil modification, seed dispersal, and predator prey. Only five of twelve species are in ex situ programs, leaving time to intervene limited.
notes: 本記事はASFの野生種（バビルサ、スラウェシイノシシ、フィリピンイボイノシシ、ヒゲイノシシ等）絶滅リスクに関する生物多様性研究の紹介であり、ヒトへの健康影響は報告されていない。中国は2018年の発生起源として言及されているのみで、記事の主題国ではないため verified_locations から除外した。

articleHeadlineTranslated: Why Is Influenza A More Frequently in the Spotlight?
articleHeadline: Mengapa Influenza A Lebih Sering Disorot?
articleSummary: Influenza A dominates seasonal disease, with A(H1N1)pdm09 and A(H3N2) circulating in humans; influenza B persists but lacks a sustained animal reservoir and pandemic potential comparable to influenza A. Notably, the B/Yamagata lineage has not been detected since March 2020, so WHO omits it from seasonal vaccines, which are now trivalent—two A components and one B/Victoria. Within A(H3N2), subclades such as clade K reflect genetic and antigenic changes in the HA gene; these do not mean a completely new virus but a diversified lineage. Indonesian experts at IDAI noted influenza A mutates rapidly in humans and across animal reservoirs. Antigenic drift—ongoing changes—occurs in A and B, while a larger antigenic shift happens only in influenza A and can spark pandemics if population immunity is low. WHO GISRS monitors these changes and updates vaccine composition twice yearly for the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, including the 2026 Southern Hemisphere trivalent formulation.
notes: 本記事はインドネシアの専門家（IDAI）のコメントを含む一般的な科学解説記事であり、特定の国での流行や症例急増などの具体的なアウトブレイク情報は含まれていない。
